stocks.note: Numbers as of market close on August 10th.
stocks.news:
A flat, slightly red day. The S&P 500 eased 0.06% to 7,753, the Dow slipped 0.11% to 53,976, and the NASDAQ gave back 0.32% to 26,605. Nothing moved much, which is its own kind of information after last week's jobs shock.

The headline number was enormous. Nvidia is teaming up with BlackRock, Blackstone, and Apollo to put $500 billion into AI infrastructure, with the investment firms lending the cash for data centers and chip capacity. Nvidia is already the most valuable public company in the world and does not need the money in any ordinary sense. What this really is: the AI buildout has outgrown what even the biggest technology balance sheets want to fund alone, so it is being financed the way pipelines and toll roads are. Nvidia still fell 2.86% on the news.

Intel went the other direction and got punished for it, dropping 4.06% after announcing a $15 billion share sale to fund AI chip factories. Selling new stock raises cash but splits ownership among more shares, so existing holders own a little less of the company. Investors read it as a company that needs money faster than it can earn it.

The two stories side by side are the whole market right now. Everyone is spending enormous sums on AI. The market rewards the ones who can borrow to do it and punishes the ones who have to sell equity.

One oddity worth a smile. Unitree, a Chinese humanoid robot maker, went public and retail investors asked for 5,526 times more shares than existed. Whatever that is, it is not calm.

feature_image.alt: Line chart of U.S. crude oil stocks in the Strategic Petroleum Reserve from August 1982 to July 2026, in millions of barrels. The reserve fills from 273 million in 1982 to a peak of 727 million in January 2010, holds near 700 million through the 2010s, then falls steeply after 2022 to 304.8 million, a level last seen in February 1983.
feature_image.caption: The Strategic Petroleum Reserve holds 304.8 million barrels as of the week ending July 31, down 58% from its January 2010 peak of 727 million and back to where it stood in February 1983. Every point is rebuilt from EIA's published weekly series; the graphic going around ends at an August 7 figure EIA has not released yet.
feature_image.source: Source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, weekly series WCSSTUS1.

economy.note: The 10-Year is the August 10 Treasury close from the daily yield curve. Gold and silver are 6:15 AM Eastern quotes on August 11 against the same hour a day earlier. Brent is the August 10 ICE front-month settlement. Stocks are as of the August 10 close and crypto is a live quote from this morning. The reserve figure is the week ending July 31, which is the most recent one EIA has published.
economy.commentary:
Oil is the story, and it runs through everything else today. Brent settled at $87.72, up 4.99% in a single session, after the White House walked back talk of a deal with Iran and said it is only semi-negotiating. Crude is now well above $87 a barrel, and the reason is simply that the shipping route stays contested.

Which brings us to the chart below. America's emergency oil reserve has been drawn down to levels not seen since the Reagan administration. The Strategic Petroleum Reserve holds 304.8 million barrels as of the week ending July 31, down from a peak of 727 million in January 2010. That is 58% below the high, and the last time the reserve held this little was February 1983, back when it was still being filled for the first time. The government has been tapping it to hold gas prices down while the Iran route is disrupted, and some analysts think it could fall to 243 million before the release ends.

A note on the number. Today's newsletter and the graphic going around both put the reserve at 298.7 million as of August 7. That week has not been published. EIA's weekly series was last updated on August 5 and its most recent figure is the 304.8 million for July 31; the August 7 week comes out tomorrow, August 12. We checked the file's own timestamp and re-pulled it to be sure. So we are reporting the last number EIA has actually released, and the 298.7 million is worth treating as a preview rather than a fact until tomorrow. The two claims on the graphic that we could check both held up: the 727 million peak is right, and the lowest since 1983 framing is true even using the published figure.

The 10-Year jumped to 4.72%, up 7 basis points, its highest of the month. Today's newsletter printed 4.70%, up 0.04; Treasury's daily curve says 4.72%, up 0.07, and we go with Treasury. This is the oil story arriving in the bond market. Expensive crude feeds into everything that gets shipped or made, which looks like inflation, and inflation is what keeps the Fed from cutting.

Metals kept climbing on the same anxiety. Gold rose 0.95% to $4,375 an ounce and silver added 1.62% to $64.96, its largest gain since Friday. The newsletter left silver out for the fifth day running.

One to file away for anyone planning a wedding. Under the new Repayment Assistance Plan, getting married can sharply raise a student loan payment, because the plan counts household income rather than just the borrower's. One example had a payment go from $146 to $730 a month. If you have first time buyers with student debt who are engaged, that is a real change to their qualifying income, and it is better discovered before the pre-approval than after.

Why a REALTOR® cares: the through line today is that oil at $87 pushes the 10-Year up, and the 10-Year is what mortgage rates follow. Last Friday's weak jobs report pulled rates down. This week's oil spike is pulling them back the other way. That is why the honest answer to when will rates drop is still that nobody can put a date on it.

crypto.note: Live quotes as of the morning of August 11 (24 hour change).
crypto.commentary:
Quiet and slightly lower. Bitcoin is near $63,784, Ether is flat at about $1,875, and XRP is just above $1.01.

The interesting move is where the money went after last week's theft. Roughly $850 million flowed into Bitcoin ETFs in a single week, and the reason is the $130 million cold wallet hack we covered on Friday. Cold storage is supposed to be the safest way to hold crypto, so when it fails, holders do not necessarily leave the asset. They move to a regulated product where somebody else carries the custody risk. That is an unusual thing for a security failure to accomplish.

Strategy, the company best known for owning enormous amounts of Bitcoin, sold $108.6 million of it to build its cash reserve to $4.65 billion. That is the second straight week it has sold and it has not bought any in more than six weeks. For a company whose entire identity is accumulating Bitcoin, a six week pause is the signal, not the sale.

real_estate.homebuilder: Mortgage Rates Ticked Up To 6.76% As Oil Jumped 5%; Nearly 8 In 10 Austin Homes Bought In 2022 Are Underwater; California, Texas And Florida Are A Fifth Of All U.S. Remodeling; Locally, 702 Homes Are Buyable, Down 13
real_estate.commentary:
Rates gave back a little. The 30-year fixed rose 2 basis points to 6.76% and the 15-year added 2 to 6.27%, undoing part of Friday's drop as oil pushed the 10-Year up. Today's newsletter printed the same two figures, matching Mortgage News Daily.

Austin is the cautionary tale, and it is worth understanding precisely. Roughly 79% of homes bought there in 2022 are now worth less than what the buyer paid, which means those owners are underwater: they owe more than the house would sell for. The cause was not a crash in demand. Builders flooded the market with new homes at the same moment mortgage rates spiked, so supply arrived exactly when buying power left.

Yesterday we covered Redfin's finding that homes now sell below asking in 38 of the 50 biggest metros, and Austin is what that looks like taken to its conclusion. It is also the clearest argument for why the Bay Area behaves differently. Austin's problem was too much new construction meeting a rate shock. We never got the construction. The same rate shock hit here and inventory simply froze instead, which is why our prices held while theirs fell.

The remodeling number is the one to actually use this week. California, Texas, and Florida together account for more than 20% of all U.S. remodeling activity. When people cannot afford to move, because selling means giving up a 3% mortgage for a 6.76% one, they renovate instead. That is the lock-in effect showing up as construction permits rather than listings, and it tells you where your seller's money is going while they wait.

Why a REALTOR® cares: there is a listing conversation in that remodeling figure. A homeowner spending $80,000 on a kitchen because moving feels impossible is a client who has already decided they want something different from their house. They are worth a real conversation about what a move would actually cost, because a lot of them have never run the numbers and are guessing at the trade.

Median asking prices: Union City at $1,298,888, Fremont at $1,288,384, Newark at $1,248,000, Milpitas at $1,150,000, and Hayward at $849,500. Median days on market runs from 22 in Newark to 35 in Hayward.

Every city except Union City lost listings today, and Union City only held even. Fremont gave up 7, Hayward 3, Newark 2, and Milpitas 1. The board wide table dropped 40 in a single day, which is the largest one day decline we have printed in weeks. Meanwhile the coming soon pipeline did not move at all, holding at 110 with Fremont carrying half of it at 55. Inventory is leaving the board faster than sellers are replacing it, and Newark is now the fastest market of the five at 22 days.
